title: Thermal pseudo-transitions in a frustrated spin-pseudospin sawtooth chain
abstract: We present an exact analysis of a spin--pseudospin X sawtooth chain that incorporates three distinct valence states of copper ions and serves as a minimal model for one-dimensional cuprates composed of corner-sharing copper triangles. The model includes magnetic exchange and electrostatic coupling constants both along the base sites and between base and apex sites capturing the competition between spin and charge degrees of freedom. Using the transfer-matrix method, we derive exact expressions for the free energy and obtain an analytical condition defining the pseudo-critical line associated with pronounced thermodynamic anomalies. The ground-state analysis reveals, besides an antiferromagnetic phase, three frustrated phases characterized by distinct residual entropies. At finite temperatures, these zero-temperature phase boundaries evolve into narrow entropy ridges signaling pseudo-transitions between the corresponding quasi-phases. The specific heat and the avoided-crossing scale exhibit sharp but continuous peaks at the pseudo-critical temperature, whereas the physical correlation length may be controlled by a different subleading eigenvalue. Local correlation functions uncover a cooperative rearrangement from charge-dominated to magnetically correlated regimes. Our results demonstrate that the sawtooth geometry promotes frustration and short-range coherence leading to pronounced pseudo-transition behavior.
summary: This work provides an exact analysis of a spin-pseudospin model mimicking cuprate chains, focusing on how geometric frustration leads to complex phase behavior. Using the transfer-matrix method, the authors identify pseudo-critical lines where thermodynamic anomalies occur due to competition between charge and spin degrees of freedom. The findings highlight that such geometry promotes short-range coherence and distinct quasi-phase transitions.
main_problem: The study investigates thermal pseudo-transitions occurring within a geometrically frustrated spin-pseudospin sawtooth chain, which models one-dimensional cuprates.
main_result: The system exhibits pronounced pseudo-transition behavior characterized by sharp but continuous peaks in specific heat and avoided-crossing scale at pseudo-critical temperatures. The geometry promotes frustration and short-range coherence.
method: The analysis relies on the exact transfer-matrix method (TMM) to derive thermodynamic properties like free energy and entropy.
model_or_system: The model is a spin–pseudospin X sawtooth chain incorporating three valence states of copper ions, capturing competition between magnetic exchange and electrostatic coupling in corner-sharing triangular units.
key_observables: Free energy, pseudo-critical line condition, specific heat, avoided-crossing scale, local correlation functions ($\langle S_i S_{i+1} angle$, $\langle \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} angle$), and residual entropies of ground states.
important_parameters: Interaction ratios like $\Delta/J$, $V/J$, and $J_1/J$; temperature ($T$) relative to pseudo-critical temperatures ($T_p$).
main_assumptions: Periodic boundary conditions are assumed for the chain length, and the transfer-matrix method is used for exact evaluation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spin-pseudospin sawtooth chain structure, the four possible ground states (AF, FR1, FR2, FR3), and temperature dependence of correlation functions across different parameter regimes.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the model and Hamiltonian, then uses TMM to derive eigenvalues and the pseudo-critical condition. It analyzes the resulting ground state phases and finally examines finite-temperature behavior, showing how zero-temperature boundaries evolve into entropy ridges signaling pseudo-transitions.
why_interesting: While focused on cuprates, the methodology of analyzing quasi-degeneracy in the transfer matrix spectrum to predict continuous but sharp thermodynamic anomalies (pseudo-transitions) is a powerful technique applicable to other low-dimensional quantum systems exhibiting competing interactions.
